The developer platform for the agentic era · entire.io

Act one

The developer problem

We made coding agents incredibly capable — and strangely forgetful.

The developer problem

Your agent forgot everything

An hour of exploration. Dozens of tools. Three hidden constraints. Two corrections. The right change, finally.

Then you close the session — and none of it follows you.

Every new session is the agent’s first day on the project.

The developer problem

This is not merely lost chat history

Every session creates real development knowledge. The code survives the session — the knowledge behind it doesn’t.

What a session creates

+The goal you were trying to accomplish
+Which files and systems mattered
+Constraints discovered along the way
+Approaches that did not work
+What the agent misunderstood — and what you corrected
+Why the implementation looks the way it does

What losing it costs

−You repeat prompts, agents repeat investigations
−Handoffs lose important context
−Reviewers reverse-engineer intent from the diff
−Strange code becomes impossible to explain
−Useful workflows stay trapped in old conversations

The developer problem

Git stores the result, not the process

Git answers

$ git log --oneline
a3f9c12 What changed? ✓
a3f9c12 Who committed it? ✓
a3f9c12 When did it happen? ✓

Agentic development asks

  • What task was this change trying to accomplish?
  • Which agent and session produced it?
  • Why was this approach selected — and what was tried before?
  • What did the developer correct?
  • Can another agent continue the work?
  • Why does this particular line exist?

If the code is worth versioning, the context that produced it is worth versioning too.

The developer problem

Agent history is fragmented

You already use more than one agent. Each tool keeps its own partial history — in its own silo.

agent·oneexploration
agent·twoimplementation
agent·threereview
ide·agentquick edits
cloud·agentbackground tasks

Should your development history belong to the agent vendor —
or to you and your repository?

Entire’s answer: context should be portable across agents and connected to the code it created.

to a developer harness

The developer harness

not the destination

Once code is connected to intent, sessions, and decisions, much richer workflows become possible.

Preserve

Coordinate

Trails · Gates

This is where Entire grows into a programmable harness for agentic development.

The developer harness

Composable primitives — not one prescribed workflow

⌘

Trails

give work a home

  • A task item linked to exactly one branch
  • Gathers intent, sessions, Checkpoints, attempts, decisions, evaluations
  • The living context while humans and agents work
▷

Runners

ask questions about the work

  • Repo-defined agent evaluations — config lives in the repository, like an Actions workflow
  • Runs ephemerally over code, intent, sessions, or a whole Trail
  • Returns an outcome — it doesn’t block anything by itself
⛨

Gates

decide the consequence

  • Enhanced branch protection
  • Can use a Runner outcome to block, require review, allow, or trigger a workflow
  • Or leave outcomes as informational health signals

Standalone by design — a Trail needs no Runners, a Runner needs no Trail, a Runner outcome doesn’t have to become a Gate. Combine them however you want.

The developer harness

Make it concrete

Trail

Replace the rate limiter without changing the public API

feature/rate-limiter
▷ task-completeness Did the implementation achieve the requested outcome? health indicator
▷ api-compatibility Has the public API changed? failure blocks
▷ performance Does it perform better under the expected load? uncertain → review

Entire doesn’t decide what “good” means. The developer defines it.

The developer harness

The future workflow

Describe outcomes. Delegate implementation. Preserve how it happened. Decide which risks need human judgment. The developer stays in control of the harness.

Infrastructure for many agents

Infrastructure

Agents create a different Git workloadpreview

  • More clones, fetches, and ephemeral environments
  • More parallel branches, higher read/write concurrency
  • More demand for regional performance

Entire’s distributed Git network mirrors repositories into regional cells built for agent-scale traffic — while you keep using GitHub.

Git was designed to be distributed. Agentic development is our chance to make software infrastructure open and distributed again.

The deck.js gives me the full picture of how it presents. Here's everything:

## Em-dashes: done

Converted 22 of 25 em-dashes in `index.html` to periods, commas, colons, semicolons, or the deck's existing `·` separator (used it where sibling items already use it, e.g. the CTA list and the SVG sub-labels). I deliberately kept three, where the pause is doing rhetorical work:

- *"incredibly capable — and strangely forgetful"* (slide 2)
- *"Then you close the session — and none of it follows you"* (slide 3)
- *"No one has figured out the final form of agentic development — yet"* (slide 21)

Say the word if you want those gone too.

## Adversarial review

**Verdict: the spine is right, the back half is overweight.** Problem → shipping product → live demo → future → invitation is the correct shape for 30–40 minutes. The timing math roughly works: ~23 slides, 5 of them fast dividers, demo ~8–10 min lands you around 35 minutes. But the risks cluster after the demo, and there's one credibility hole.

### The structural problems

**1. The demo is your energy peak, and 11 slides follow it — nearly all speculative.** Acts 3–5 are entirely future-tense (Trails, Runners, Gates, the Git network, principles). After a live demo, an audience's attention drops fast when everything becomes "will be." This is the single biggest risk in the track. Fix by cutting Act 3 from four slides to three and compressing Acts 4–5 (below).

**2. Act 4 is one slide wearing an act costume.** A full divider (slide 18) for a single content slide (the Git network) undermines the five-act structure and burns ~90 seconds of transition on a topic that's marked "preview" anyway. Same for Act 5: a divider plus principles plus CTA. Proposal: drop the Act 4 and Act 5 dividers, fold the network slide into the end of Act 3 as "and the infrastructure underneath all of this," and let principles → CTA → close run as the natural landing.

**3. The network slide is a scope grenade.** Nineteen slides into a talk about *context and memory*, you pivot to *distributed Git hosting*. It reopens "wait, what is this company?" right when you should be converging. If you keep it (the "while you keep using GitHub" line does defuse the scariest read), keep it to 90 seconds and bridge it explicitly from Runners: ephemeral agent evaluations *need* fast regional clones. If the talk runs long in rehearsal, this is the first cut.

**4. Four problem slides is one too many.** Slides 3–6 all argue the same thing. Slide 4 ("not merely lost chat history") overlaps heavily with slide 3's punchline and slide 5's pull-quote — and slide 5's *"If the code is worth versioning, the context that produced it is worth versioning too"* is the actual thesis of the talk. Proposal: cut slide 4 (narrate its left column over slide 3's terminal animation) and let slide 5 land harder, sooner.

**5. Redundant flowchart.** Slide 17 ("The future workflow") redraws what slides 14–16 just established — the progression graphic on 14 and the flow SVG on 17 are the same pipeline twice. Cut 17; slide 16's concrete Trail card is a much better closer for Act 3.

### Content-level issues

- **Slide 10: eight capability cards is a wall.** Nobody reads eight cards while you talk. The "Cross-agent skills" card also duplicates slide 9's read-path chips. Cut to six, ideally the ones your demo will echo.
- **Slide 11: seven negations is defensive.** "A GitHub replacement, *today*" is a wink that will hijack Q&A — people will ask about the "today" instead of your product. Either own that intentionally or trim the list to the 3–4 negations that kill real misconceptions (agent, proxy, prompt manager).
- **Slide 21: eight principles is a manifesto wall.** Five max; group or cut. Principles 1, 2, 3, and 7 overlap substantially (they're all "open and portable").
- **Slide 8 wording:** "code and its **production context**" reads as "the prod environment." You mean "the context that produced it" — worth rephrasing.
- **Slide 6:** the answer line deflates the rhetorical question the moment it appears. Make `frag-a` a `data-fragment` so the question hangs for a beat before you reveal Entire's answer.

**The credibility hole: nothing addresses secrets and privacy.** You're proposing to store agent transcripts — prompts, tool output, corrections — *in the repository, forever*. The first hostile question is guaranteed: "my sessions contain API keys, internal URLs, and half-baked opinions about coworkers — that's in git history now?" There is no slide, bullet, or beat that answers it. Add one line to slide 9's architecture (what's captured, what's redacted, what never leaves the machine) or prepare a crisp Q&A answer. Right now this is the gap a skeptic will drive a truck through.

### Presenter mechanics (from deck.js)

- **No blackout key.** You'll be switching to a terminal for the live demo; add a `B` key that blanks the stage so the deck isn't glowing behind your demo window. One-line addition to the keydown handler.
- **No speaker notes.** For 30–40 minutes with a demo in the middle, you may want at least a printed outline; the deck has no notes mode.
- Re-entering a slide replays its entrance animations (`show()` forces a reflow deliberately) — fine forward, slightly janky if you back up mid-talk. Not worth fixing unless it bugs you in rehearsal.

### Proposed track (≈19 slides, ~33 min + Q&A buffer)

| Segment | Slides | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Title + Act 1 (cut slide 4) | 5 | 6 min |
| Act 2 (trim slide 10 to 6 cards, slide 11 to 4 items) | 5 | 6 min |
| Live demo | 1 | 8–10 min |
| Act 3 (cut slide 17) + network slide folded in | 5 | 7 min |
| Principles (trim to 5) + CTA + close, no dividers | 3 | 4 min |

Want me to apply any of these cuts, add the blackout key, or make slide 6's answer a fragment? All are quick.
